commons:4451723.summary: In the margin beside the Greek psalm text, Christ hangs on the cross in a blue colobium while one soldier lifts a sponge on a pole and another a lance. Below, a deliberately parallel scene shows a dishevelled iconoclast pushing a similar sponge on a pole against a round icon of Christ to blot it out, with a bowl at his feet. The page equates the destruction of holy images with the insults offered to Christ at his Passion, a passionate defence of the icon made soon after the end of Iconoclasm.
facts: The miniature illustrates the psalm verse 'They gave me gall to eat; and when I was thirsty they gave me vinegar to drink' (Psalm 69:21; 68 in the Septuagint).
The iconoclast is identified as John the Grammarian, the last iconoclast Patriarch of Constantinople, caricatured with wild, straight hair.

The Chludov Psalter is one of only three illuminated Byzantine psalters surviving from the 9th century; it was taken from Mount Athos in 1847 and later passed to the State Historical Museum in Moscow.
commons:4451723.notes: Commons names both John the Grammarian and Patriarch Anthony I; only one iconoclast figure is clearly visible here, and Wikipedia identifies him as John the Grammarian. Folio number not verified. This is a polemical image and should be presented as such.
commons:4451723.original_title: Iconoclasts John Grammaticus and Anthony I of Constantinople

wga:zearly/1/2mural/1domitil/domitil1.summary: In this arched lunette of the Catacomb of Domitilla, a young, beardless Christ sits at the centre in a white tunic and pallium, larger than the figures around him, while apostles in pale robes are ranged on either side in a shallow arc. At the lower left stands a box of scrolls, and Christ himself appears to hold a scroll, signs of his authority as teacher. Images like this presented Christ as the true philosopher instructing his followers, a theme that would grow into the majestic apse compositions of later churches.
facts: Although often published (including by the Web Gallery of Art) as a 2nd-century 'Last Supper', no table or food is shown; the scene is more commonly read as Christ teaching among the apostles, and only part of the twelve appear.
Scenes of Christ seated among the apostles belong mainly to the 4th century in the Roman catacombs, which is why a 2nd-century date for this lunette is doubtful.
The Catacombs of Domitilla are among the largest in Rome, extending for some 17 km on several levels.
wga:zearly/1/2mural/1domitil/domitil1.notes: WGA title 'Last Supper' and date '2nd century' look unreliable: no meal is depicted, and comparable 'Christ among the apostles' scenes date to the 4th century (some sources give c. 350–375, others late 3rd–early 4th). Re-titled and re-dated cautiously; the precise cubiculum was not confirmed.

wga:zearly/1/4mosaics/2ravenna/4nuovo/5t.summary: On a shimmering gold ground, Judas leans in to kiss a bearded, haloed Christ, who stands calmly in a purple mantle at the centre of the panel. From the left soldiers with spears and torches press forward, one reaching for Christ's shoulder, while on the right the apostles look on; one of them grips a sword, recalling Peter's attempt to defend his Master. The scene belongs to the cycle of Christ's Passion along the upper wall of the nave, among the earliest extended narrative sequences of the Passion in monumental art.
facts: Theodoric the Great built Sant'Apollinare Nuovo as his Arian palace church; it was dedicated in 504 to Christ the Redeemer.
The upper band of the south (right) wall holds thirteen Passion and Resurrection scenes, in which Christ is bearded, whereas in the miracle scenes on the opposite wall he is young and beardless.
The cycle omits the Flagellation and the Crucifixion itself.
wga:zearly/1/4mosaics/2ravenna/4nuovo/5t.notes: WGA gives only '6th century'; the upper-tier Christological panels belong to the Theodorician decoration (before 526). The precise year is not known.
